concept.name: Code Mental Health / Codebase Wellbeing
concept.definition: A non-clinical engineering metaphor for the condition and sustainability of a software repository: whether maintainers can see problems, discuss them without blame, make safe changes, recover from regressions and receive enough time and peer support to maintain the system.

source_inspiration.title: Депресія — тема табу? Ознаки депресії, міфи довкола антидепресантів, як допомогти собі
source_inspiration.transcript_coverage: The supplied excerpts cover 00:00–00:07:55 and 01:17:16–01:19:53 only; most of the middle is unavailable.
source_inspiration.adaptation_note: The video discusses human mental health. This repository borrows only broad communication and support themes as an explicitly metaphorical prompt for software-maintenance culture. It does not convert clinical concepts, symptoms, diagnoses or medication into software metrics, and it does not claim that the video contains software-engineering advice.

principles.principle: Make it safe to say that something is wrong.
principles.engineering_translation: Treat failing tests, regressions, warnings and incidents as evidence to investigate, not as grounds for shaming the person who reported them. Preserve logs and reproducible steps.

principles.principle: Do not hide difficult topics or work.
principles.engineering_translation: Track technical debt, unsupported modules, flaky tests and unowned components in ordinary project workflows. Make the work visible without turning counts into personal performance scores.
Record architecture decisions, incident timelines, migration notes and postmortems so knowledge does not remain trapped with one contributor.

principles.principle: Asking for help is a normal engineering action.
principles.engineering_translation: Provide code review, pair debugging, issue escalation and maintainer hand-off paths. Avoid making one person the only route to understanding critical code.

principles.principle: Build support before the system is in trouble.
principles.engineering_translation: Keep tests, backups, release notes, rollback procedures and reproducible development environments available before a high-risk change is shipped.
Reserve capacity for dependency updates, refactoring, documentation, flaky-test repair and removal of obsolete paths instead of treating feature throughput as the only measure of progress.

support_model.purpose: A repository needs reachable maintainers and more than one person who understands critical components.
A team needs protected time and a planned budget for routine care.
examples: time for refactoring and flaky-test repair

support_model.purpose: Repeatable checks and clear documentation reduce avoidable uncertainty.
High-impact changes need the right reviewers and explicit recovery plans.

engineering_myths.myth: A green CI run proves that the software has no defects.
engineering_myths.correction: CI proves only that the configured checks passed for that run and environment. Coverage, design flaws, missing scenarios and production conditions remain outside that evidence.

engineering_myths.myth: A larger test count automatically means better confidence.
engineering_myths.correction: Test relevance, determinism, failure diagnosis, boundary coverage and maintenance matter more than raw test count.

engineering_myths.myth: A linter or static analyzer can replace code review.
engineering_myths.correction: Tools detect selected patterns. They do not fully assess intent, usability, architecture, threat models or operational context.

engineering_myths.myth: An AI-generated patch means the root cause is fixed.
engineering_myths.correction: Generated changes still need a reproduced failure, causal explanation, focused tests, review and a rollback path.

engineering_myths.myth: A complete rewrite is always healthier than incremental repair.
engineering_myths.correction: Rewrites can discard operational knowledge and introduce new failure modes. Compare migration risk, compatibility, testability and rollback options.

engineering_myths.myth: TODO and FIXME markers are a reliable defect score.
engineering_myths.correction: Markers are prompts for triage. Their meaning, age, owner, context and impact must be reviewed by a maintainer.

dimensions.interpretation_limit: Heuristic review cues only; file size and marker count do not prove poor design or a defect.
Presence does not prove adequate coverage, test quality or passing status.
File presence does not prove that documentation is accurate or current.
A name in a file does not prove availability, capacity or healthy team dynamics.
A written process does not prove that rollback has been rehearsed or will succeed.
Manifest presence does not prove dependencies are current, safe or supported.
Documents are evidence of a process, not proof that learning has been applied.

reporting_rules: Report observed evidence and its source path; do not infer hidden project state.
Use observed, missing or unknown for each signal; avoid an overall mental-health score.
Treat TODO/FIXME/HACK/XXX and large-file counts as review prompts, never automatic defects.
Do not label a repository, contributor or team as depressed, sick, burned out or otherwise clinically described.
Keep scans read-only, bounded and local; do not upload source code or telemetry.
explicit_non_goals: No human mental-health assessment, screening, diagnosis or risk prediction.
No inference about contributors from commit timing, activity, language, audio or device telemetry.
No productivity ranking, contributor scoring or individual blame.
No automatic rewrite, deletion, dependency update or remediation without human review.
No claim that a static repository scan proves code correctness, security or maintainability.
